newsitem.title: USA: U.S. seen backing a Raytheon-Hughes merger.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seen backing a Raytheon-Hughes merger.

text.p: If General Motors Corp. directors approve the sale of Hughes Electronics' defence operations to Raytheon the government will take a close look but ultimately permit the deal, analysts said Thursday.

Encouraged by the Department of Defence and spurred by the shrinking money available for military expenditures, one consolidation has followed another in the defence industry and the latest is no surprise, they said.
"It's just a continuation of the trend," said Gordon Spivack, an anti-trust lawyer with Coudert Bros. in New York.

So far the government has approved most deals, including such consolidations as the Lockheed-Martin merger. Still on the table is the proposed Boeing McDonnell-Douglas merger, which Attorney General Janet Reno said Thursday will be considered by the Federal Trade Commission.

Many analysts wondered if the government would permit a Hughes-Raytheon deal without changes in the missile division, because the combined entity would have 80 to 90 percent of the missile business in the United States.
"There will be some significant scrutiny of this area," said Joe Campbell, an analyst at Lehman Brothers in New York.
Bob Skitol, a Washington anti-trust attorney in the firm of Drinker Biddle & Reath, said "The missile overlap will be addressed one way or another."
Skitol said the government may require a spin-off or some licensing that "would at least provide the possibility of some other defence supplier becoming a missile vendor."
Nonetheless, the Defence Department itself has made it easier for companies to merge by agreeing to have taxpayers pick up some of the costs of consolidation.
The government "has made some consolidation costs allowable under Defence contracting rules," said Rich Golaszewski, who heads GRA Inc., a Jenkintown, Pa., consulting firm.
With such strong encouragement from the Department of Defence, the FTC and Justice Department have tended to allow mergers, anti-trust attorneys said.
"They're dealing with it pragmatically rather than on the basis of law," said Spivack. "They're bending over backwards to give discretion to the Department of Defence."

Golaszewski said the bottom line is that the "new fad" among managers is to sell non-core business units, taking the view that "If you can't be Number One or Number Two don't be in it because you can't make money."

On any such deal, the Defence Department reviews the proposed merger and makes a recommendation to the Federal Trade Commission or Justice Department. The two agencies decide among themselves which one will review the deal.
As a practical matter, all of the recent military mergers have been reviewed by the FTC and analysts said they would expect a Raytheon-Hughes deal to be as well.
